# Terminology {#sec-terminology}

Definitions are grouped by subject and link to their fuller treatment. The [alphabetical index](index-alphabetical.qmd) provides the same terms A–Z.

![The lexicon's spatial vocabulary anchored across two scales: a parcel-scale plan (siting-led restoration) and an array-scale section (structure- and management-led restoration), with the footprint as the shared anchor between them. Structure terms are drawn in charcoal; the [restorative functions](restorative-functions.qmd) appear in color at their physical homes. The conceptual naming terms defined below, including agrisolar, ecovoltaics, dual use, and LER, have no single element to point to.](../figures/fig_terminology_scales.svg){#fig-terminology-scales}

## Scale {#sec-terms-scale}

Developed in [§-@sec-transect, The Scale Transect](scale-transect.qmd).

### Scale Transect {#term-scale-transect}

A single gradient from farmstead (A1) to regional (A5) that most other terms are read against, defined by covarying attribute bundles rather than capacity thresholds. See [The Scale Transect](scale-transect.qmd).

*Borrowed, and turned.* The device is the rural-to-urban Transect of the New Urbanism [@dpz2014], which is where the lexicon takes its name and its method of calibration points. One thing changes in the borrowing, and it matters: that transect is a gradient across the ground, a line you could walk from wilderness to urban core, while this one is a gradient of project size. Two A2 projects can sit a mile apart, and an A5 can surround an A1.

### A0 — the zero-land case {#term-a0}

Arrays mounted on buildings, which take no ground at all: no siting latitude to spend, no ground layer to design, and no [siting axis position](#term-siting-axis) to hold. It sits at the transect's origin rather than on it. See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

### A1 — Farmstead {#term-a1}

<100 kW, under about an acre; behind-the-meter, single owner-operator, existing farm labor and equipment. See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

### A2 — Field {#term-a2}

100 kW–1 MW, roughly 0.5–8 acres; behind-meter to distribution, landowner with possibly one lease counterparty. See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

### A3 — Parcel {#term-a3}

1–5 MW, roughly 6–30 acres of array; distribution, community solar or mid-market PPA, multi-party, purpose-built ground management. Big enough that management arrives and small enough to site deliberately, which makes it the only zone carrying both restorative instruments at once and the widest part of the [feasible wedge](#term-feasible-wedge). Often called **community-scale solar**, a phrase carrying several senses at once: sized to a community's load, sited where communities already are, structured so benefit reaches a community, and building community resilience through a distributed fleet. See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) and [§-@sec-community-scale](scale-transect.qmd#sec-community-scale).

### A4 — Landscape {#term-a4}

5–50 MW, roughly 30–300 acres; developer-led institutional capital, contract-enterprise ground management. The widest band on the transect, and it probably contains a jurisdictional break near 20–25 MW, the capacity at which several states move siting from local boards to a state office. Not split yet (§-@sec-open-issues, issue 1). See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

### A5 — Regional {#term-a5}

50 MW+, from roughly 300 acres to 10,000 and beyond; transmission, utility or IPP across jurisdictions, contract enterprise at ranch scale. Open-ended by design. See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

### Siting latitude {#term-siting-latitude}

The designer's freedom over where the array goes. What governs it migrates from opportunistic placement to land assembly and grid topology up the transect, and it peaks at A2–A3, bounded by the parcel at A1 and by the land market at A5. The constraint that makes the feasible region a [wedge](#term-feasible-wedge). See [Design Levers](design-levers.qmd#sec-lv-mode) for the modes against the levers, and §-@sec-restoration-modes for which one dominates at each zone.

### Restoration mode {#term-restoration-mode}

Which [design lever](#term-design-levers) a design commits to carry the restorative work: the choice of ground, the array's geometry, how the array is run, who holds the asset, or what the parties signed. Each mode names a lever, so there are five modes for six levers. Scale has none, because deciding how big to build is not itself a way of doing restorative work, only what settles which ways stay available. The first three are done on the ground and shift along the transect as siting latitude rises and falls (§-@sec-restoration-modes). The last two are done on paper and trade against each other: ownership-led is free at the farmstead and unavailable at utility scale, and contract-led runs the opposite way. Five modes:

- []{#term-siting-led}**Siting-led** — the restorative work is done by the choice of ground; requires the A2–A3 latitude to choose it.
- []{#term-structure-led}**Structure-led** — array geometry does the work: clearance, row spacing, module transmissivity.
- []{#term-management-led}**Management-led** — placement is a given, and the ground cover, grazing regime, and operational schedule carry everything. The dominant mode at A4–A5.
- []{#term-ownership-led}**Ownership-led** — the work is done by who holds the asset, and no agreement is needed because the parties were never opposed. Strongest at A1–A2, where the operator owns both the array and what stands under it, and effectively unavailable once the owner is absentee.
- []{#term-contract-led}**Contract-led** — the work is done in the lease, the ordinance, or the benefit agreement rather than anywhere on the site. The mode the [community and economic function](#term-fn-community) runs on, and the one that decides whether the tenant is still farming in year twenty (§-@sec-fn-community).

See [Design Levers](design-levers.qmd#sec-lv-mode) for the modes against the levers, and §-@sec-restoration-modes for which one dominates at each zone.

### Stocking density {#term-stocking-density}

Instantaneous animals per unit area at a moment; diverges from carrying capacity with forage growth, utilization, and climate. A grazing design variable to calibrate, not a fixed rate. See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-grazing).

### Carrying capacity {#term-carrying-capacity}

The season-long forage the land sustains over time, distinct from instantaneous [stocking density](#term-stocking-density). See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-grazing).

### Contract grazing {#term-contract-grazing}

Grazing delivered as a contracted vegetation-management service by a party who does not live on site; appears at A3 and scales up into a logistics enterprise. See [§-@sec-zones](scale-transect.qmd#sec-grazing).

## Sharing and sparing {#sec-terms-sharing}

Developed in [§-@sec-siting-axis, The Siting Axis](siting-axis.qmd).

### Siting Axis {#term-siting-axis}

The second, largely scale-independent dimension: whether the array shares land with agricultural production (**land sharing**), spares land by taking ground out of it (**land sparing**), or neither. The pair is borrowed from conservation ecology [@green2005; @phalan2011]; the short form *sharing–sparing* is used for the axis, the full form in prose. Five positions, centered on S3. See [The Siting Axis](siting-axis.qmd).

### S1 — Full sharing {#term-s1}

Production continues within the array footprint, in the same ground, as in vegetable [agrivoltaics](#term-agrivoltaics), crops between rows. See [§-@sec-positions](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

### S2 — Functional sharing {#term-s2}

The ground layer is productive but subordinate to the array, as in grazing or forage. Available at every scale, and with S3 the spine of the [feasible wedge](#term-feasible-wedge). See [§-@sec-positions](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

### S3 — Coexistence {#term-s3}

Neither sharing nor sparing: the array takes ordinary ground outright and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise holding it, so the restoration is socioeconomic before it is biophysical. The center of the axis, and where most projects sit. See [§-@sec-positions](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

### S4 — Idled-land sparing {#term-s4}

The array occupies ground already idle, marginal, or out of production, so that productive land is spared; the benefit accrues to the land *not* taken. See [§-@sec-positions](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

### S5 — Impaired-land retirement {#term-s5}

Production ends on ground that carried a measurable off-site burden such as chronically low yields, high runoff, nutrient or pesticide export, irrigation draw beyond the aquifer's budget, or on ground positioned where that burden can be intercepted. The removal acts on the ground taken itself. See [§-@sec-positions](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

### Bare conversion {#term-bare-conversion}

Ordinary ground converted with the farm operation ended: the same ground fact as S3 without the restorative one. The non-restorative baseline the axis is read against, not a position on it. See [§-@sec-positions](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

### Feasible wedge {#term-feasible-wedge}

The feasible region across scale and sharing, shaped like a lens: all five positions open at A3, closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes, at A5 as land assembly and build cost remove the poles, at A1 as in-footprint farming and meaningful sparing both need more scale to be real. Each thinned corner has a documented exception. See [§-@sec-wedge](siting-axis.qmd#sec-wedge).

## Pressures and levers {#sec-terms-pressures}

Developed in [§-@sec-pressures-ch, Design Pressures](design-pressures.qmd).

### Design pressures {#term-design-pressures}

The competing forces every site must resolve. Unlike axes they have direction, they conflict, and real parties advocate for them. Nine are named. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Energy yield {#term-energy-yield}

Pressure: maximize energy per unit land. Pushes toward dense row spacing, optimal tilt and tracking, low clearance, whole-field coverage. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Build cost {#term-build-cost}

Pressure: minimize installed cost per watt. Pushes toward standard racking, low clearance, minimal ground preparation, conventional geometry. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Operations and maintenance {#term-operations-maintenance}

Pressure: minimize management burden across a 25–40 year asset life. Pushes toward uniform, mowable or gravel ground cover, and can oppose build cost, since native seeding raises capex and lowers long-run opex. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Agricultural production {#term-agricultural-production}

Pressure: keep working land working. Pushes toward high clearance, equipment access, production [ground layers](#term-ground-layer), farmer contracts. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Restorative goals {#term-restorative-goals}

Pressure: make ecological, hydrological, and economic resilience a design objective co-equal with generation. The pressure this document exists to advance, and still a force among forces. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Community acceptance and benefit {#term-community-acceptance}

Pressure: secure and sustain community acceptance *and* community benefit, two forces that can come apart, held under one name because they have to be advanced together. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Grid and market demands {#term-grid-market}

Pressure: satisfy whoever is buying the power, the attributes, or the tax position. The channel through which outside parties push their requirements onto a design. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Policy and permission {#term-policy-permission}

Pressure: satisfy the rules that decide whether the project happens at all, and the subsidies that decide what pays. Permitting path and zoning, prime-farmland and setback rules, state programs, and federal incentives. It is the one pressure whose direction is set by the jurisdiction rather than by the site or the buyer, which is why it belongs to [regionality](design-pressures.qmd#sec-regionality) as much as to §3. See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### End-of-life responsibility {#term-end-of-life}

Pressure: minimize the residual footprint left after a 25–40 year asset life and preserve the option to return the ground to its prior use. For the end-of-life vocabulary itself, see [Decommissioning / Repowering / Reversibility](#term-decommissioning). See [§-@sec-pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

### Design levers {#term-design-levers}

The six kinds of decision a project can actually make, and the only things anyone can change: **scale**, how much ground it takes; **siting**, which ground; **structure**, what gets built; **management**, what grows and how the place is run; **ownership**, who holds the asset; and **contracts**, what the parties signed. The first four act on ground and are limited by scale, and the last two act on paper and are not. Which lever carried the restorative work is the [restoration mode](#term-restoration-mode). See the [Design Levers](design-levers.qmd) chapter, and [§-@sec-siting-latitude](scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) for the levers read against the transect.

## Restorative functions {#sec-terms-functions}

Developed in [§-@sec-functions, Restorative Functions](restorative-functions.qmd).

### Restorative function {#term-restorative-function}

A restorative capacity a project can be designed to deliver, obtainable to varying degrees from many structural positions at once, the columns laid over the archetypes as rows (§-@sec-functions). Four are biophysical, one agricultural, and one socioeconomic. See [Restorative Functions](restorative-functions.qmd).

### Hydrologic function {#term-fn-hydrologic}

Water quantity and quality as design objectives. On **quantity**: infiltration and recharge raised, soil moisture buffered, and at scale consumptive use retired from a basin's budget. On **quality**, two routes needing opposite ground: **avoided loading**, siting on the ground that is doing the leaching, which the water-quality literature calls a critical source area, so the fertilizer and pesticide programs stop with the cropping, and **interception**, siting on the flow path below it so runoff gives up its nutrients and sediment before reaching a channel. See [§-@sec-fn-hydrologic](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-hydrologic).

### Soil & carbon function {#term-fn-soil}

Perennial, low-disturbance cover rebuilding soil organic carbon and aggregate stability under and between the panels, against a construction-disturbance debt paid first. See [§-@sec-fn-soil](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-soil).

### Ecological function {#term-fn-biodiversity}

What can live on the ground and what can move through it. Habitat is built from the ground layer up, through floral resources, nesting substrate, and vegetation structure, with mowing and grazing *timing* as decisive as the seed mix; [connectivity](#term-connectivity) is the other half. Reachable across S2–S5, which is why it is a function and not a position. See [§-@sec-fn-biodiversity](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-biodiversity).

### Connectivity {#term-connectivity}

Whether organisms can move into, through, and out of a site, as against whether the site can feed them once they arrive. It is designed at four scales at once: inside the array by fencing, roads, and mown strips; at the edge by whether the planting meets an existing corridor; across a landscape by the choice between a few large arrays and many small ones; and at regional range by whether a fleet of sites falls within dispersal distance of one another. Connectivity is a property of the arrangement rather than of any one patch, and the scale on which it matters is set by the disperser, so a connectivity claim means little until it names the taxon. See [§-@sec-fn-biodiversity](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-biodiversity).

### Agricultural function {#term-fn-agricultural}

What the array does *for* farming, on its own ground and on the fields around it: pollination and pest regulation carried by the ground layer beyond the fence, forage and stock shelter under the panels, and the lease revenue that keeps the operation running. Not the [siting axis](#term-siting-axis) restated, which records whether production continues in the footprint rather than what the project gives farming. Its dominant [benefit delivery](#term-benefit-delivery) runs along living things, which makes it the function most dependent on what surrounds the site. See [§-@sec-fn-agricultural](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-agricultural).

### Community & economic function {#term-fn-community}

The one socioeconomic function: the economic prosperity, livability, and health and equity a project builds for its host, the [SCALE](#term-scale-footprint) Communities domain read as an outcome, and distinct from the [social-license](#term-community-acceptance) pressure and [community-benefit](#term-community-benefit) lever that aim at it. Only legible once the recipients are named separately. See [§-@sec-fn-community](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community).

### Benefit delivery {#term-benefit-delivery}

How a function's benefit reaches whoever receives it. The useful question is not how far it goes but **which route it takes**, since nearly every function reaches from the panel to the region along some path. Three routes. **In place**, where provider and beneficiary are the same ground. **Along a connection**, where the benefit travels a network: water carries runoff, sediment, and recharge downslope; living things carry pollination, pest regulation, and dispersal; paper carries lease, tax, and subscription along tenure, contract, and jurisdiction. And **[by preservation](#term-displaced-benefit)**, where nothing moves and the benefit is ground elsewhere that stayed as it was. The route decides who can verify a claim and who captures it. See [§-@sec-benefit-range](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-benefit-range).

**Prior names.** The distinction is borrowed, not coined. @hernandez2019 call an outcome that overlaps the generation site *sympatric* and one spatially separated from it *disjunct*, and assign each a *serviceshed*, the largest ecological scale at which it contributes goods and services. This lexicon splits the disjunct side into bands and adds delivery by preservation, which a service-based scheme cannot express.

### Delivery by preservation {#term-displaced-benefit}

The mode in which a benefit consists of ground nearby remaining as it was. It is what [land sparing](#term-s4) delivers. It is proximate, because a developer assembling acreage near a substation chooses among parcels within a fairly narrow radius, so the ground spared is realistically ground in the same county. What it is not is observed: the claim rests on a counterfactual, and it is tested against the local land market and the sites genuinely in play rather than against an unbounded alternative. See [§-@sec-benefit-range](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-benefit-range).

### Co-benefit {#term-cobenefit}

The field's usual word for what this lexicon calls a [restorative function](#term-restorative-function). Recorded here because it is what practitioners will say, and used here only to describe how others frame the same ground. The term carries acknowledged definitional ambivalence, and its grammar demotes what it names, since a *co-*benefit arrives alongside the real objective [@mayrhofer2016]. This document argues these capacities are objectives, so it does not adopt the word. *Cf.* **techno-ecological synergy**, the literature's own attempt at a framing that does not subordinate them [@hernandez2019].

### SCALE footprint {#term-scale-footprint}

A whole-project reading across four domains, Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, and Energy, each running from causing harm at the rim, through avoiding harm, to promoting benefit at the center (§-@sec-harm-benefit). Evaluative by design, but the ring where harm ends is a zero point rather than a pass mark. See [Restorative Functions](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale).

## Archetypes {#sec-terms-archetypes}

Developed in [§-@sec-archetypes, Archetypal Forms](archetypes.qmd).

### Archetype {#term-archetype}

A recurring way the [design pressures](#term-design-pressures) have been resolved at a particular scale zone and sharing position, carrying particular functions. Used in its plain sense, meaning a characteristic, transformable pattern rather than an exhaustive set. See [Archetypes](archetypes.qmd).

### Overhead and interspace systems {#term-overhead-interspace}

The engineering standards' hardware typology (DIN SPEC 91434; the NREL / InSPIRE configuration taxonomy): *overhead* systems mount modules above the working surface, *interspace* systems mount them low with the crop or cover between the rows. It classifies the structure, where an archetype classifies the resolution of pressures. See [Archetypes](archetypes.qmd).

## Regionality {#sec-terms-regionality}

Developed in [§-@sec-regionality, Regionality](design-pressures.qmd#sec-regionality).

### Regionality {#term-regionality}

The claim that the [design pressures](#term-design-pressures) resolve differently in different places, because the factors that weight them vary across space. The vocabulary is constant everywhere; which positions are available, which functions are reachable, and how hard each pressure pushes are not. See [Regionality](design-pressures.qmd#sec-regionality).

### Regional factors {#term-regional-factors}

The six spatial factors the lexicon reads a region by: the **resource** (sun and cloud, including diffuse fraction), the **grid operator** (queue, curtailment, and the state programs that decide whether A3 exists), **aridity** (which flips the sign of the shade effect), **latitude** (which sets tilt, row spacing, and the inter-row light budget), the **cropping system** (which decides whether sharing is conceivable), and **irrigation** (which makes retirement at scale available or unavailable). See [§-@sec-rg-factors](design-pressures.qmd#sec-rg-factors).

### Regional calibration {#term-regional-calibration}

A restatement of the lexicon's indicative values for a particular region: capacity bands, absent zones, the binding constraint, the positions realistically open. The US calibration in §-@sec-rg-us is one such, not the general case; calibrations from other regions are additions rather than corrections. See [§-@sec-rg-us](design-pressures.qmd#sec-rg-us).

### Design import {#term-design-import}

The characteristic regional failure: carrying a resolution from the region where it was demonstrated into one whose factors differ, as when a shade benefit shown in the Southwest is assumed in the Midwest, a habitat specification calibrated on one establishment cost written into a contract for another. [Grid and market demands](#term-grid-market) is the usual vehicle, since a buyer's criterion travels further and faster than the evidence behind it. See [§-@sec-rg-consequences](design-pressures.qmd#sec-rg-consequences).

### Diffuse fraction {#term-diffuse-fraction}

The share of irradiance arriving as diffuse rather than direct-beam light. Cloud collapses the beam component while diffuse holds up, so humid and cloudy regions run a higher diffuse fraction of light, which is non-directional, reaches under and between panels, and is most of what a [ground layer](#term-ground-layer) lives on. It also weakens the case for tracking. See [§-@sec-rg-factors](design-pressures.qmd#sec-rg-resource).

## Field terms and metrics {#sec-terms-field}

The vocabulary the lexicon adopts from the wider field and pins down for use here.

### Agroenergy {#term-agroenergy}

Energy infrastructure sited and designed to interact intentionally with agricultural or ecological land function. Umbrella term, not solar-specific.

*Term collision, flagged deliberately.* Elsewhere "agroenergy" (and *agro-energy*) most often means agriculture-*derived* **bioenergy**: energy crops, crop residue, biogas, and biomass, meaning farmland as a fuel source. This lexicon repurposes the word for the converse: energy *infrastructure* placed on and integrated with agricultural land. The reuse is intentional but worth naming, so a reader arriving from the bioenergy literature is not misled. The infrastructure sense is live in the peer-reviewed literature: @stid2025 define agrisolar as the integration and co-management of solar photovoltaics, agriculture and ecosystem services **within agroenergy landscapes**.

### Agrisolar {#term-agrisolar}

Agroenergy specific to photovoltaics. This lexicon uses it as a neutral umbrella across the [siting axis](siting-axis.qmd), including S3–S5 rather than only agricultural co-location. **Multi-use solar** is a related, narrower term covering agrivoltaics, rangevoltaics, and ecovoltaics [@merheb2025].

**Syn.:** multi-use solar (narrower: excludes S3–S5 without an ecological ground layer).

### Agrivoltaics {#term-agrivoltaics}

Crop or livestock production within the array footprint (S1–S2). Crop response to shade is climate- and crop-dependent; a synthesis of 367 paired observations found yield response turning positive only in hotter conditions [@merheb2025].

**Syn.:** agrophotovoltaics (German); photovoltaic agriculture (Chinese); solar sharing (Japanese).

### Rangevoltaics {#term-rangevoltaics}

Grazing under and between panels, read here as [functional sharing](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions) (S2). The everyday name is **solar grazing**; the literature also uses *rangevoltaics* [@merheb2025]. Species and clearance must be matched to the racking, which in practice means sheep (§-@sec-siting-latitude). Shade is also a benefit that can be a requirement: Humane Farm Animal Care certification mandates shade where temperatures run consistently above 22 °C, which makes an array a compliance instrument as well as a pasture.

**Syn.:** solar grazing.

### Ecovoltaics {#term-ecovoltaics}

Solar development that co-prioritizes ecosystem function with generation through siting, layout, ground-layer design, operations, and a viable business model [@sturchio2023; @tolgyesi2023]. This lexicon treats its ecological ground layer as a [restorative function](restorative-functions.qmd), not an axis position. The framework favors repair of disturbed ground over conversion of intact native ecosystems [@sturchio2025croplands].

::: {.caution}
**The definitional dispute.** AFT advances a production-based definition of dual use; critics argue it excludes ecosystem benefits and imposes a one-size-fits-all instrument on farmland protection. Both terms are defined precisely above, and both map to positions on the [siting axis](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions), which locates the disagreement where it belongs, as a genuine conflict between agricultural production and restorative goals (§-@sec-conflicts) rather than as a misuse of words. This document describes that dispute; it does not adjudicate it.
:::

**Source:** @sturchio2023 — [Sources](sources.qmd).

### Dual Use {#term-dual-use}

A production-based term: co-location that keeps *active agricultural production* within the array footprint across the project's life, which is American Farmland Trust's criterion. Structurally a mandate for [S1–S2](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions). Distinct from [ecovoltaics](#term-ecovoltaics), whose ecological ground layer is a function rather than production; the two are the poles of the definitional dispute the lexicon holds open rather than adjudicates (§-@sec-wedge).

### Restorative {#term-restorative}

The frame of this entire lexicon rather than a dimension within it. Applied when ecological, hydrological, or economic ground-layer function is a design objective co-equal with generation, not an incidental byproduct. US arrays are designed primarily to maximize output and minimize cost; co-benefits arrive incidentally or through a patchwork of state and local policy [@hernandez2014; @mccall2023]. *Restorative* names the deliberate alternative.

*Borrowed, and worth placing.* The word comes from restorative design [@reed2007], where it sits one rung below *regenerative*: restorative returns a system to health, regenerative leaves it able to keep renewing itself. The lexicon keeps that modesty deliberately and widens the scope, so the word covers hydrologic, agricultural, and community function and not ecology alone. It is not the solar trade's *site restoration*, which is what a decommissioning plan owes when a lease ends, and not restoration to a reference ecosystem in the sense ecological restoration uses. The compound *restorative agrisolar* is the lexicon's own.

### Co-location vs. Integration {#term-colocation-integration}

The pair that makes [agrisolar](#term-agrisolar) the superset and [agrivoltaics](#term-agrivoltaics) one member of it.

**Co-location** — solar and an agricultural land use share a landscape without functional interdependence. @stid2025 call this *lateral* or *adjacent* co-location: agricultural land is replaced, and the two sit side by side.

**Integration** — the two share the same ground and the same light: panel height set by livestock clearance, row spacing by forage light requirements, tracking schedule by photosynthetic timing. @stid2025 call this *vertical* or *coincident* co-location — agrivoltaics proper.

Read against the axis, that is the whole set relation in one line: **integration is [S1–S2](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions); co-location without integration is S3 and below.** Agrivoltaics is the integrated subset of agrisolar, which is why this document needs the wider word.

Integration is also the line a design crosses to be restorative in the structural sense rather than in name only, though S3 is the reminder that a project can restore an enterprise without integrating anything.

*Usage caution:* @stid2025 use "agrisolar" in two senses: broadly, for the superset covering both cases, and narrowly, where "agrisolar co-location" means the adjacent case alone. **This lexicon uses the broad sense throughout.**

### Footprint vs. Influence Zone {#term-footprint-influence}

**Footprint**: land physically occupied by racking, panels, access infrastructure. **Influence Zone**: the larger, typically asymmetric area whose hydrology, microclimate, soil, wildlife movement, or visual presence (viewshed) is measurably affected. The solar-siting literature already splits *footprint* the same way, into the **array/direct footprint** (panels and racking) versus the **facility/fenceline footprint** (the whole permitted parcel), and the ecovoltaic siting research makes the distinction matter: several small sites carry higher aggregate edge-to-area ratio than fewer large ones, amplifying both inward effects (pesticide drift) and outward ones (pollination, pest control). **Fragmentation geometry is a first-order design variable.**

The zone can also act through *economics* rather than through hydrology or sightlines. @stid2025 document intentional fallowing of irrigated cropland **adjacent to** arrays, 968 ha across 58 utility-scale installations in California's Central Valley, about 27% of those arrays' own area, apparently funded by array revenue, and call the practice **solar fallowing** where the aim is reducing water use. The array changes what happens on ground it never occupies.

Its multi-domain accounting across Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, and Energy is the [SCALE footprint](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale), introduced with the restorative functions (§-@sec-functions).

### Screening {#term-screening}

The management of the array's outward visual presence: perimeter setbacks, vegetative buffers (hedgerows, tree/shrub belts), earthen berms, fencing treatment, and glint/glare control. It acts on the *visual* portion of the [Influence Zone](#term-footprint-influence). Screening is dual-function, since the same vegetative buffer that buys [community acceptance](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) can carry habitat and connectivity value, so it is pushed by both community acceptance and restorative goals, while costing generation (edge shade), land, and sometimes agricultural production; its habitat value is greatest where the surrounding landscape is otherwise bare of hedgerows. Descriptive only: the lexicon names the lever, not a required buffer width, berm height, or setback.

### Community Benefit {#term-community-benefit}

The instruments through which a project returns value to its host community: community-benefit or host-community agreements (CBA / HCA), payments in lieu of taxes (PILOT) and tax revenue, good-neighbor / abutter payments, community-solar subscription, local hiring, co-ownership or locally-owned models, and decommissioning bonds as a community-protection instrument. Distinct from acceptance: benefit and acceptance can come apart, since benefit without a fair process can read as a bribe, so the [community acceptance](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) pressure holds both as forces in tension rather than treating a check as consent.

### Microclimate {#term-microclimate}

The array's reshaping of the near-surface energy balance: shade lowers daytime soil and canopy temperature and the vapor-pressure deficit under the panels, while longwave sheltering lifts nighttime minima, so the microenvironment swings less far across the day [@sturchio2023; @pinos2026; @barrongafford2019]. It is a **mechanism rather than a [function](#term-restorative-function)**, and the lexicon stopped listing it as one because its results are already counted elsewhere: retained moisture is the water function, thermal refuge is ecology, and relief for a shade-tolerant crop, shelter for stock, and shade for the people working there are agriculture. Its sign flips with climate and crop, and it is carried by the [structure](#term-design-levers) lever throughout. See [§-@sec-functions](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-functions).

### Ground Layer {#term-ground-layer}

Whatever occupies the surface beneath and between panels. Primary carrier of restorative function. The solar and agronomic literatures also call this the **understory** or the **ground cover** / **vegetation layer**; "ground layer" is used here because it stays neutral about whether that surface is planted, grazed, gravelled, or bare.

**Syn.:** understory; ground cover; vegetation layer.

### Marginal / Previously Disturbed Land {#term-marginal-land}

The low-value ground that [idled-land sparing](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions) (S4) presupposes: consistently low-yielding cropland, and previously disturbed land such as reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brownfields ("brightfields"). Marginality is partly a property of the ground and partly of the market, so claims of marginal-land siting deserve scrutiny about what fraction of a footprint is genuinely marginal (§-@sec-wedge).

### Pore Space {#term-pore-space}

*(borrowed)* — The three-dimensional volume between modules and between modules and ground. Names the thing that "panel height" and "row spacing" only hint at, and treats it as habitat and working room rather than leftover gap.

**Source:** @toledo2021 — [Sources](sources.qmd). Toledo & Scognamiglio's "descriptive model towards a sustainable landscape vision" is a direct predecessor to this lexicon's own describe-the-landscape stance, reading array geometry through landscape-ecology's patch–matrix–corridor lens rather than as a yield problem alone.

### Ground Coverage Ratio (GCR) {#term-gcr}

The ratio of module area to total ground area, which is the density of the array. High GCR packs more capacity per acre and pushes with energy yield and build cost; low GCR opens the [pore space](#term-pore-space) and inter-row that agrivoltaics and a working ground layer need. GCR is the single number behind much of the row-geometry ↔ ground-layer coupling (§-@sec-siting-latitude).

### Module Technology {#term-module-technology}

The panel itself as a [structure lever](design-levers.qmd#sec-lv-ground): *monofacial* vs *bifacial* (both faces generate); *vertical bifacial* (east–west, leaving the inter-row open to machinery, extending sharing to larger scale [@vaverkova2026]); *semitransparent / transmissivity-tuned* (passing some light to a crop below); and *spectrally selective* (transmitting the wavelengths plants use while harvesting the rest). Module choice sets how much light, and of what kind, reaches the [ground layer](#term-ground-layer).

### Tracking Schedule & Curtailment {#term-tracking-curtailment}

Two [management levers](design-levers.qmd#sec-lv-ground). *Tracking schedule* is how a single- or dual-axis array is steered through the day, normally to maximize generation, but an ecovoltaic operation may orient panels partly for the light, water, or temperature reaching the ground [@knapp2024]. *Curtailment* is the deliberate reduction of output for grid, price, or ecological reasons. Both are decisions about how the array is *run*, the instrument of management-led restoration at A4–A5 (§-@sec-siting-latitude).

### Land Equivalent Ratio (LER) {#term-ler}

The standard dual-use productivity metric: the land a monoculture would need to match what the co-located system yields on one unit of ground (LER > 1 = a land-productivity gain). It captures *production* co-yield well but is silent on ecological, hydrologic, and community function, and it handles the non-production ground layers of [S3–S5](siting-axis.qmd#sec-positions) poorly and has no term for the [restorative functions](restorative-functions.qmd) or the [SCALE](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale) domains beyond food and energy. Its blind spots are given alongside it because it is the metric most likely to be taken as the measure of success by default. No single success metric is endorsed here (§-@sec-open-issues, issue 5).

### Decommissioning / Repowering / Reversibility {#term-decommissioning}

The end-of-life questions a 25–40-year asset raises: *decommissioning* (removing the array and restoring the ground), *repowering* (replacing modules to extend the site), and *reversibility* (how completely the prior land use can return). Foundation type, soil disturbance, and financial assurance (decommissioning bonds) set how reversible a project is; reversibility is often the crux of the farmland-protection argument, and is itself one of the nine [design pressures](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (§-@sec-pressures).

## The trade's vocabulary {#sec-terms-trade}

Terms the lexicon uses but does not own. They come from the solar industry, from utility practice, and from the USDA soil survey, and they are given here in the sense a developer or a county planner would use them, so that a reader meeting one in these pages is not sent elsewhere to find out what it means.

### Interconnection {#term-interconnection}

The physical and legal connection between an array and the electric grid: the line it ties into, the equipment that ties it, and the utility's permission to energize. The wait in an interconnection queue routinely runs years, and it commonly settles a project's size and its site before any design question is asked.

### Substation {#term-substation}

The facility where voltage is stepped between distribution and transmission. Nearness to one is the siting criterion farming does not share, which is why it pulls large arrays toward ground chosen for the grid rather than for the soil.

### Offtake {#term-offtake}

The contract naming who buys the power and at what price: a utility power purchase agreement, a corporate buyer, a subscriber list, or the farm's own meter. It sets project size more directly than the solar resource does.

### Behind-the-meter {#term-behind-the-meter}

Generation serving a load on the customer's side of the utility meter, so the power offsets a bill rather than being sold. The milking parlor, the cold store, and the well pump are behind-the-meter loads.

### Utility-scale {#term-utility-scale}

Not a fixed threshold. In ordinary use it means an array selling wholesale rather than serving a local load, which begins somewhere above [A3](#term-a3) and is routine at [A4](#term-a4) and [A5](#term-a5). Berkeley Lab splits its two national datasets at 5 MW-AC.

### Community solar {#term-community-solar}

A distribution-connected array whose output is subscribed by households and businesses that cannot host panels of their own. Program caps commonly sit at 5 MW, which is one reason [A3](#term-a3) tops out where it does. The phrase carries at least four distinct meanings in current circulation (§-@sec-community-scale).

### Clearance {#term-clearance}

The vertical gap between the ground and the lowest edge of a panel. It decides what can work underneath, from nothing at all, to sheep, to a tractor, and buying more of it costs steel. The lexicon names clearance as a lever and declines to fix a number for it.

### Row spacing {#term-row-spacing}

The distance from one row of panels to the next, normally measured centerline to centerline rather than as the open gap between rows. With clearance it settles what equipment can work inside the array, and with panel size it sets the [ground coverage ratio](#term-gcr).

### Racking {#term-racking}

The steel carrying the modules: posts, beams, and the fasteners between them. Foundation type, usually driven pile, ground screw, or surface ballast, governs how much soil is disturbed at construction and how completely the ground can be returned at [end of life](#term-decommissioning).

### Tracker {#term-tracker}

Racking that rotates the modules through the day, almost always about a single north–south axis. Trackers raise output and cost, need more room between rows, and their rotation schedule is a design lever in its own right, because it decides how much light reaches the ground and at what hour.

### Mass grading {#term-mass-grading}

Reshaping an entire site with earthmoving equipment before construction, rather than setting foundations to the existing contour. It is the most consequential single decision for soil carbon and site hydrology, and it is usually taken on cost grounds.

### Land assembly {#term-land-assembly}

Putting together enough contiguous acreage, often across several owners, to make a large project financeable. It is what removes [siting latitude](#term-siting-latitude) at [A4](#term-a4) and [A5](#term-a5): the array lands where parcels could be assembled near a [substation](#term-substation), not where the ground most wanted it.

### Prime farmland {#term-prime-farmland}

A USDA classification for land whose physical and chemical properties can sustain high yields under ordinary management. It is a property of the soil map unit rather than of the field's realized yield, which is why a parcel classed prime can still carry persistently unproductive ground (§-@sec-community-scale).
